name: Tukuche
tagline: The old salt-trade capital of the Thakali, under Dhaulagiri
meta_description: Tukuche, the Thakali salt-trade village of the Kali Gandaki at 2,590 m: merchant houses, gompas, a distillery, the Thak library and Dhaulagiri views.
summary: Tukuche is a Thakali village at about 2,590 m in the Kali Gandaki gorge, 13 km south of Jomsom. It was the chief trading post of the salt trade between Tibet and the Nepal hills, and its large merchant houses, gompas and small museum tell that story. Dhaulagiri and Tukuche Peak rise straight above it.
intro: Tukuche looks too big for where it is. Along its lanes stand tall three-storey houses with carved wooden windows, inner courtyards big enough for a caravan of mules, and heavy wooden doors. They were built by Thakali merchant families who grew rich when Tukuche was the main market of the Kali Gandaki salt trade, where salt from Tibet was weighed, taxed and traded for rice and goods from the south.

That trade faded in the 20th century, and many families moved to Pokhara, Kathmandu and beyond. What remains is one of the most interesting villages in Mustang to walk through slowly. There are several gompas, a small local distillery that makes fruit brandies, the Thak library and a museum on Thakali life, plus orchards running down to the river. Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) and Tukuche Peak (6,920 m) rise above the western side of the valley.

Few visitors stop for long, which is why we like it. Tukuche makes a calm overnight on a walk down the Kali Gandaki from Jomsom and Marpha, or a half-day visit by jeep. The deepest stretch of the Kali Gandaki gorge, the section between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I, lies about 7 km further south near Lete, so Tukuche is also a good base for understanding the scale of this valley.

story.title: Where Tibetan salt met hill-country rice
paras: For centuries salt was the most valuable thing that came over the Himalaya. It was dug from dry lakes on the Tibetan plateau and carried south on the backs of yaks, sheep and mules, down through Lo and the Kali Gandaki. Grain, sugar, cloth, iron and later manufactured goods went north the other way. Somewhere along the valley the two flows had to meet, be weighed and be taxed. From the 19th century that place was Tukuche, in the heart of the Thakali country the Thakali call Thak Khola.

In the second half of the 19th century, under the Rana government in Kathmandu, Thakali merchant families won the contract to collect customs on the salt trade through Thak Khola. With it came control over much of the trade itself. The leading families carried the title subba, built the great houses that still line Tukuche's lanes and sent their sons to study and trade in Kathmandu and India. For several decades Tukuche was one of the wealthiest villages in the Nepal hills, until the contract system ended around the late 1920s.

The final blow came after 1959, when the border with Tibet was tightened and Indian salt arrived by road and rail to the plains. The caravans dwindled and many Tukuche families followed the trade south, opening hotels, shops and the Thakali kitchens now found all over Nepal. The village population fell. Today some families have returned to restore their houses, run lodges and keep up the gompas, and Thakali from across Nepal come back for clan rituals and festivals. The great houses are still here, waiting.

people: Tukuche is a Thakali village in Thak Satsae, the old Thakali heartland south of Jomsom, and the best-known Thakali clan names, Sherchan, Tulachan, Bhattachan and Gauchan, belong to this part of the valley. Many households have moved to Pokhara or Kathmandu, but keep their ancestral houses and return for festivals and clan rituals. Those who stay run lodges, orchards, the distillery and small shops. Thakali and Nepali are spoken; most people also know some Tibetan.

untold.fact: The Kali Gandaki directly between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I, about 7 km downstream from Tukuche, flows at around 2,520 m, roughly 5,570 m below the summit of Annapurna I. By that measure the gorge is often called one of the deepest in the world.

From the late 19th century until about the late 1920s, Thakali merchant families held the government contract for customs on the Thak Khola salt trade, which made Tukuche the main trading post between Tibet and the Nepal hills.
Tukuche Peak, the 6,920 m mountain rising west of the village, is one of the high summits that pilots must fly beside on the Pokhara–Jomsom route, because the small planes cannot fly over the range.

taste.name: Phapar roti
taste.text: Phapar roti is a flat buckwheat bread, dense and nutty, cooked on a griddle and eaten with butter, honey, chutney or a spoon of local jam. Thakali lodges in Tukuche serve it at breakfast; ask the day before so the family can make it fresh.

facts: ≈ 350 km · 2 days by road via Pokhara and Beni
Salt-trade history, Thakali merchant houses, gompas, distillery, Dhaulagiri views

highlights.title: The merchant houses
highlights.text: Walk the lanes past three-storey Thakali houses with carved windows, large inner courtyards and stables for caravan animals. Some are restored and lived in; others stand empty. Your guide can explain which families built them and how the trade worked.

highlights.title: Gompas of Tukuche
highlights.text: The village has several small gompas, including Rani Gompa and Sambha Gompa, with old statues and wall paintings. Most are looked after by caretakers rather than resident monks, so go with a guide who can find the key.

highlights.title: Tukuche distillery
highlights.text: A small local distillery makes brandies from apples, apricots and other fruit grown in the valley. Ask to see the stills and buy a bottle direct. Tastings are informal and depend on who is around, so plan for the morning.

highlights.title: Thak library and museum
highlights.text: The Thak library and the small museum on Thakali life display household objects, trade tools, clothing and photographs from the salt-trade years. They give context to the houses you walk past. Opening hours depend on caretakers; check current status locally.

highlights.title: Dhaulagiri from the riverbank
highlights.text: Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) and its icefall rise above the west side of the valley, with Tukuche Peak alongside to the north. The view is best at dawn from the riverbank, before cloud builds and the afternoon wind blows dust up the valley.

highlights.title: Walk to Marpha
highlights.text: An easy 2-hour walk north along the Kali Gandaki brings you to Marpha, passing orchards and the Tibetan settlement at Chhairo on the east bank. Walking north means the afternoon wind is behind you, the easiest direction in this valley.

how_to_reach.text: Tukuche is on the Beni–Jomsom road, ≈ 13 km south of Jomsom (30–40 minutes by jeep) and ≈ 145 km from Pokhara (7–8 hours by jeep via Beni, Tatopani and Ghasa). Local buses stop on the road beside the village.
Fly Pokhara–Jomsom (about 20 minutes, early morning only), then drive south 30–40 minutes. In bad weather, the road from Pokhara is the backup.
Tukuche is about 2 hours' walk south of Marpha, or 4 hours from Jomsom, on the Kali Gandaki trail. From the south, it is a day's walk up from Kalopani or Lete.

where_to_stay: Tukuche has a handful of family-run lodges, some in restored merchant houses with wooden interiors and courtyards. Rooms are simple, with shared or attached bathrooms and a warm dining room in the evening. There is no high-end hotel. For a comfortable base, stay in Jomsom at Shinta Mani Mustang or Om's Home, 30–40 minutes away by jeep, and visit Tukuche for half a day. If you are walking the valley, a night here between Marpha and Kalopani is the more rewarding choice.
tips: Go with a guide who knows the village; most gompas and the museum are kept locked and need a caretaker.
Walk north towards Marpha rather than south, so the afternoon wind is at your back.
Ask permission before entering courtyards of the merchant houses; many are still private homes.
Buy brandy or dried fruit here as a direct way to support families who have stayed in the village.
Photograph Dhaulagiri at sunrise; by mid-morning cloud often builds on its south face.

experiences.title: Salt-trade houses of Tukuche with a local guide
experiences.summary: A two-hour walk through Tukuche's lanes with a guide from the valley, looking at the merchant houses, caravan courtyards and gompas built in the salt-trade years, and hearing how a small Thakali village came to control much of the trade between Tibet and Nepal.
body: We begin on the main lane, where the houses are biggest. Your guide will show you how they were built for trade: large ground-floor courtyards where mule and yak trains could unload, storerooms for salt and grain, family rooms above, and flat roofs for drying crops. Carved wooden window frames and heavy doors show the money that once flowed through here. Some houses are restored and lived in; some have been empty for decades.

As we walk, the story of the salt trade comes together. Tibetan salt came south through Lo and Kagbeni; grain, cloth and sugar went north. From the late 19th century, Thakali merchant families held the government contract for customs on this trade, and Tukuche was the main market. The leading families were known by the title subba. You will hear names of families whose descendants now run hotels and businesses across Nepal.

We visit one or two of the village gompas, such as Rani Gompa or Sambha Gompa, depending on which caretaker is home, and stop at the Thak library or the small museum if they are open. The walk ends with tea in a lodge kitchen. If you want to go deeper, Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf's book Himalayan Traders (1975) covers the Thakali trade in detail. Wear shoes you can slip off easily for the gompas.

faqs.q: Why was Tukuche important in the salt trade?
faqs.a: Tukuche sat at the meeting point of the trade between Tibet and the Nepal hills. Salt from the Tibetan plateau came down the Kali Gandaki, and grain and goods went up. From the late 19th century, Thakali families held the customs contract for this trade, and Tukuche became its main market, which made its merchant families very wealthy.

faqs.q: Can I go inside the old houses in Tukuche?
faqs.a: Some, with permission. Several merchant houses are now lodges, so staying overnight is the easiest way to see one from inside. Others are private homes or locked and empty. A local guide can often arrange a visit to a courtyard or a restored room. Always ask before entering, and do not climb on fragile roofs or balconies.

faqs.q: Is there a museum in Tukuche?
faqs.a: Yes. Tukuche has a small museum on Thakali life and the Thak library, with household objects, trade tools, clothing and photographs. They are modest and kept by caretakers, so hours vary and they may be closed in winter. Your guide can usually arrange access; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Tukuche distillery and Mustang fruit brandy
experiences.summary: Visit the small distillery in Tukuche that turns the valley's apples, apricots and other fruit into brandy, see the stills, and taste the result. A short stop that pairs well with the village walk and supports one of the businesses that keeps people living here.
body: Fruit growing came to the Kali Gandaki valley in the second half of the 20th century, after the salt trade declined. Apples and apricots grow well in the cold, dry climate between Tukuche and Jomsom, and distilling turned surplus fruit into something that keeps and travels. Tukuche's distillery is one of the best-known producers in the valley, and its bottles are sold in shops and lodges from Jomsom to Pokhara.

On a visit you see the simple process: fruit is crushed and fermented in tanks, then distilled in copper or steel stills and rested before bottling. In autumn you may see fresh fruit coming in from the orchards. Production is small and seasonal, so what is on show depends on the month, and someone needs to be there to open up. The scale is small, a few rooms and a handful of people, which is part of its appeal.

Tastings are informal, a small glass of apple or apricot brandy. Bottles are sold on site. We usually combine this stop with the village walk, ending here before lunch. As with any alcohol at altitude, keep it small if you are going higher the next day. Visits are subject to the distillery being open; we confirm the day before. Bottles are heavy, so plan around flight baggage limits from Jomsom.

faqs.q: What does Tukuche distillery make?
faqs.a: It makes fruit brandies from fruit grown in the Kali Gandaki valley, mainly apple and apricot, and sometimes other fruit depending on the harvest. Bottles are sold at the distillery and in lodges and shops around Jomsom, Marpha and Pokhara. Range and availability change by season, so ask what is current when you visit.

faqs.q: Can I visit Tukuche distillery without a booking?
faqs.a: You can try, but it is a small operation and someone needs to be present to show you around. We call ahead the day before. Late morning in autumn is the best time, when fruit is coming in. Outside the season, you may only be able to buy bottles.

faqs.q: Is Tukuche brandy the same as Marpha brandy?
faqs.a: They are similar spirits made from the same valley's fruit, but by different producers with their own recipes and strengths. Marpha brandy is the better-known name nationally; Tukuche's distillery is a separate producer. Tasting both on a walk down the valley is part of the fun, though small glasses are wise at this altitude.

experiences.title: Dhaulagiri sunrise from the Kali Gandaki
experiences.summary: Get up before dawn and walk to the riverbank below Tukuche to watch first light reach Dhaulagiri, the world's seventh-highest mountain at 8,167 m, with Tukuche Peak and the Dhaulagiri icefall above the valley. A quiet hour before the wind and the jeeps.
body: Dhaulagiri rises about 5,500 m above the floor of the Kali Gandaki here, one of the greatest vertical rises anywhere on earth. From Tukuche you look straight up at its eastern flank, with the Dhaulagiri icefall pouring down between the peaks and Tukuche Peak (6,920 m) to the north. In the half-light before dawn the snow is grey and blue; the first sun turns the summit pink, then gold. It is a sight few trekkers stay for.

We leave the lodge about 30 minutes before sunrise with a torch and walk down to the gravel bars of the river, a few minutes away. In October and November the sky is usually clear; in spring there can be haze. It is cold at dawn at any time of year, often below freezing, so bring a down jacket, hat and gloves, and a flask of tea from the lodge.

After sunrise we walk back for breakfast as the light fills the valley. Photographers should bring a telephoto lens for the summit and a wide lens for the valley. By 10 am cloud often builds on the mountain and the wind begins, so the morning is the only reliable window. This pairs well with the village walk and distillery visit later in the day. In winter, the light comes later and the cold is sharper, but the air is often clearest.

faqs.q: Can you see Dhaulagiri from Tukuche?
faqs.a: Yes. Tukuche is one of the best places in the Kali Gandaki valley to see Dhaulagiri (8,167 m), which rises steeply above the west bank, with Tukuche Peak and the Dhaulagiri icefall. The view is clearest at sunrise from October to December. By mid-morning, cloud often hides the summit.

faqs.q: How cold is sunrise in Tukuche?
faqs.a: At dawn in autumn and spring, temperatures are usually around −2 to 5 °C; in December and January they can drop to −10 °C. The wind is usually calm at dawn, which helps. Wear a down jacket, hat, gloves and warm shoes, and bring a hot drink. Temperatures rise quickly once the sun reaches the valley.

faqs.q: Is Dhaulagiri the mountain above Jomsom?
faqs.a: Dhaulagiri is visible from much of the Kali Gandaki valley, but it stands on the west side further south, above Tukuche and Larjung. The snow peak directly above Jomsom is Nilgiri. From Tukuche you see Dhaulagiri close and full height, which is why we recommend sunrise here rather than in Jomsom.

experiences.title: Walk into the deepest stretch of the gorge
experiences.summary: A full-day walk south from Tukuche through Larjung and Kobang to Kalopani and Lete, into the stretch of the Kali Gandaki that lies between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I. The valley narrows, pine forest returns and both 8,000 m peaks loom on either side.
body: South of Tukuche the valley changes. We walk through Kobang and Larjung, Thakali villages with stone houses and narrow lanes, and the dry hills slowly give way to pine and juniper as the rain shadow weakens. The river runs in a wide gravel bed, and on clear days Dhaulagiri rises to the west and the Annapurna massif to the east, each more than 5,000 m above you. The air feels softer as you descend.

About 7 km below Tukuche the river passes directly between Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) and Annapurna I (8,091 m) at around 2,520 m. Measured from those summits down to the river, this stretch is often described as one of the deepest gorges in the world. The valley floor here is still a few kilometres wide, so the depth is something you feel from the mountains on either side rather than a narrow canyon.

We reach Kalopani or Lete in the afternoon, about 6–7 hours of walking with a gentle loss of height, and stay in a lodge there. From Kalopani, jeeps run back up to Jomsom or down to Beni and Pokhara. This walk suits travellers who want to see how the land changes from the dry trans-Himalaya to the green hills in a single day. Luggage goes ahead by jeep, so you carry only a daypack.

faqs.q: Is the Kali Gandaki the deepest gorge in the world?
faqs.a: By one measure, yes. Between Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) and Annapurna I (8,091 m) the river flows at about 2,520 m, around 5,570 m below Annapurna I. Using that measure, from summit to river, the Kali Gandaki is often called one of the deepest gorges in the world. Other measures, using the canyon walls themselves, rank other gorges deeper.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Tukuche to Kalopani?
faqs.a: It is about 15–18 km and takes 6–7 hours, losing a few hundred metres of height. The trail follows the river through Kobang and Larjung, partly on village paths and partly near the road. It is not technically difficult but it is a full day, so start early and carry water, snacks and a windproof.

faqs.q: Can I take a jeep back after the gorge walk?
faqs.a: Yes. Kalopani and Lete are on the Beni–Jomsom road, and jeeps run north to Jomsom (about 1.5 hours) and south to Beni and Pokhara. We arrange a private jeep to meet you at the end of the day, or a lodge in Kalopani if you prefer to stay the night and see the peaks at sunrise.

faqs.q: What is Tukuche known for?
faqs.a: Tukuche is known as the old capital of the Thakali salt trade. Its large merchant houses with carved windows and inner courtyards were built by families who controlled trade between Tibet and the Nepal hills. Today it is also known for its distillery, small gompas, the Thak library and close views of Dhaulagiri.

faqs.q: How far is Tukuche from Jomsom?
faqs.a: Tukuche is about 13 km south of Jomsom on the Beni–Jomsom road, 30–40 minutes by jeep. On foot it is about 4 hours via Marpha, which is roughly halfway. Many visitors walk Jomsom to Marpha one day and Marpha to Tukuche the next, with luggage carried by jeep.

faqs.q: Is Tukuche worth an overnight stay?
faqs.a: Yes, if you like quiet villages and history. Tukuche has few visitors, family lodges in old houses and the best close sunrise view of Dhaulagiri in the valley. One night lets you walk the lanes in the evening, see the peaks at dawn and visit the gompas and distillery before moving on.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Tukuche?
faqs.a: Yes. Tukuche lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so foreigners need an ACAP permit (NPR 3,000; SAARC nationals NPR 1,000) and a TIMS card. No restricted area permit is needed. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers in conservation areas must walk with a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Tukuche?
faqs.a: Tukuche sits at about 2,590 m, slightly lower than Marpha (2,670 m) and Jomsom (2,700 m). It is a comfortable height for most people, though you may notice it on stairs and on the first night. Nights in autumn are near freezing, and in winter they fall well below zero.

faqs.q: Who lives in Tukuche?
faqs.a: Tukuche is a Thakali village in Thak Satsae, the old Thakali heartland of the Kali Gandaki south of Jomsom. Families here carry clan names such as Sherchan, Tulachan, Bhattachan and Gauchan. Many families now live in Pokhara or Kathmandu but keep their houses here and return for festivals and rituals.

faqs.q: Is Tukuche on the Annapurna Circuit?
faqs.a: Yes. Tukuche is on the Kali Gandaki section of the Annapurna Circuit, between Marpha and Kalopani. Many trekkers now skip this section by jeep, which means the trail and village are quieter than they were before the road. Walking it gives you Thakali villages, orchards and close views of Dhaulagiri.

faqs.q: Can I see the Kali Gandaki gorge from Tukuche?
faqs.a: Tukuche is inside the gorge. The deepest section, where the river flows directly between Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I, is about 7 km downstream near Lete. From Tukuche you see Dhaulagiri rising straight above the valley. Walk south to Kalopani for the full sense of depth between the two peaks.

faqs.q: What should I eat in Tukuche?
faqs.a: Eat Thakali food. Lodges serve the Thakali khana set of rice or dhido with black lentil dal, vegetables, pickles and ghee, as well as buckwheat bread (phapar roti), apple products and local brandy. Thakali cooking is famous across Nepal, and eating it in its home valley is part of the visit.
